title: The Bishop's Opening
setupTitle: Four moves, then pick a plan

setup.label: Bishop to c4, aimed at f7
Then: bishop to g5, or pawn to f4

beats.say: After e4 e5, almost everyone plays knight to f3. The Bishop's Opening puts the bishop on c4 first and leaves that knight at home on purpose.
That one change keeps two roads open: the queen's road to h5, and the f-pawn's road to f4. A knight on f3 would block both.
Most club players have never studied it. They see an undeveloped knight and an uncastled king, think you're doing it wrong, and try to punish you.
We'll build the setup, learn two attacking plans, then two sharper d4 gambits. These ideas come from GM Igor Smirnov's video, retold in our words and checked with Stockfish.

beats.card: Four moves, then pick a plan
beats.say: Four moves, then one decision. Watch the list tick itself off.
Pawn to e4, and Black answers with e5.
Bishop to c4, straight at f7. That square is guarded only by Black's king, and this bishop will matter in every trap you see today.
Black's most natural reply: knight to f6, hitting your e-pawn.
Guard it with the d-pawn. Quiet, but it also opens a road for your dark-squared bishop.
Black copies with bishop to c5, and your queen's knight comes out. This setup is often called the Vienna Hybrid.
Now look at what you didn't do. The g1 knight is still home, so the queen can reach h5 and the f-pawn can reach f4.
Black's next move picks your plan. If they castle, pin the knight with bishop to g5. If their king stays in the middle, push the f-pawn.

chapters.title: Plan A: they castle
chapters.from: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Bc5 Nc3

beats.say: Black does the most natural thing in chess and castles.
Their king is now committed to the kingside. That's what makes the pin strong.
Bishop to g5 pins the knight to the queen. With the king already castled, pushing g5 to chase your bishop would open Black's own king.
Black asks the bishop where it's going.
The safe answer is bishop to h4. The pin stays on, and the engine calls it level.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Bc5 Nc3 O-O Bg5 h6
beats.say: The bold answer is pawn to h4. Go on, take my bishop.
To be honest, this one is a trap, not a rule. If Black just ignores it with d6, the engine likes Black slightly. Play it when you want the risk.
But most players take. You take back, the knight is hit, and your rook now looks straight up the open h-file.
Where can the knight go? Your pieces cover d5, e4, g4 and h5. So it has to go backward, to e8 or h7.
Say it goes to h7.
Queen to h5. Queen and rook stack up on the h-file, and Black can't hold h7 for long.
Black makes an escape square on f8 for the king.
Take f7 with check first. Your bishop guards the queen, so the king can't take it. It has to go to h8.
Now give up the rook on h7. The king has to take it.
Queen back to h5. Checkmate.
One warning. After the rook recaptures on g5, Black's only good move is d5, which hits back in the centre. Then it's level and you play chess.

chapters.title: Plan B: they play d6
chapters.from: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Bc5 Nc3

beats.card: King in the middle: push the f-pawn
beats.say: This time Black plays d6 and keeps the king in the middle.
Now the pin is less scary for them, so switch plans.
Pawn to f4. It's like a King's Gambit, but your c1-bishop guards the pawn, so it isn't even a gambit.
This is why the knight waited. On f3 it would have blocked this pawn. It comes out next, adding a third hit on e5.
If Black takes, they give up the centre and your bishop develops with a gain of time. That's just good for you.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Bc5 Nc3 d6 f4
beats.say: The tricky reply: knight to g4. Black threatens bishop to f2 check, or knight to f2 forking queen and rook.
Push f5 anyway. The pawn cuts the c8 bishop off from g4, so now your queen threatens to take that knight.
Most players go ahead with the fork. It's a mistake: the engine now has you about one and a half pawns ahead.
Leave the rook. Queen to h5, together with the bishop on f7. Mate is threatened.
Castling stops that mate. It walks into the next one.
Bishop to g5 hits the queen. Black can't block with f6, because your bishop on c4 pins that pawn to the king.
The queen steps to e8. Knight to d5. Let Black take the rook; you're counting attackers, and you have more.
Knight to f6, check. Black has to take it, or queen takes h7 is mate.
Bishop takes back. The king has no pawns left in front of it.
Black grabs another piece. Queen to g5, checkmate.
The honest note: after queen to h5, Black's best is g6, and you're about a pawn and a half better. That's still a very good start.
Want more? Instead of guarding e4, offer it. Pawn to d4.
Black has two captures. One is fine. The other one loses, and it's the natural one.
Knight takes e4, the pawn it was already attacking. That's the wrong one.
Pawn takes e5. Already about plus one for White, and that knight in the middle is going to be chased.
Black hits f2 and feels like the attacker. That's the real mistake.
Queen to d5 hits three things: mate on f7, the knight on e4, and the bishop on c5 behind it.
Black takes on f2 with check. Step the king to f1. Nothing has changed: f7 and e4 are both still hit.
Castling stops the mate, and you take the knight. You're a piece up, and your attack is just starting.
Develop, then bishop to d3. Queen and bishop now point at h7.
Black blocks with g6. Bishop to g5 comes in and hits the queen.
Bishop to f6. It locks the king in and owns the dark squares around it.
Queen to h4, heading for h7 and h8.
Black plugs the h-file with h5.
Queen takes h5 anyway. A queen sacrifice.
Black takes. Knight to g5, and nothing stops bishop to h7.
Bishop to h7, checkmate, with the knight guarding it.
Now the correct capture: pawn takes d4.
Don't take back yet.
Knight to f3 first. This is the Urusov Gambit. The engine calls it level, which is a fair price for fast development.
Your e-pawn is unguarded now, and most players grab it.
Queen takes on d4 and hits the knight. You're a pawn down, but every piece of yours is about to join in.
If the knight drops to d6 and hits your bishop, let it.
Castle. Black takes the bishop, and the rook checks on the e-file. You're a piece down. Watch.
Black blocks with the bishop, which was the only guard of g7. Queen takes g7 and hits the rook.
The rook hides on f8. Bishop to h6, and it can't be saved: queen takes f8 is next. You're winning.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nf3 Nxe4 Qxd4
beats.say: The better retreat is back to f6. Then you develop and aim everything at the king.
Knight to c3, then bishop to g5 pins the knight.
Knight to c6 hits your queen. Slide her to h4, toward the king Black is about to castle.
If Black plays h6 here, you can ignore it. The pawn can't take your bishop, because that opens the h-file and your queen takes the rook.
Black castles. You castle long. A pawn down, but every piece is out and your rook is on the open file.
Bishop to d3. Now bishop takes f6, then queen takes h7, is a threat.
Black pushes h6. Sacrifice the bishop there anyway.
Queen takes back. The king's pawn cover is gone.
Knight to g5 brings one more attacker toward h7. The engine says you're winning by a mile.
Some players simply copy you: bishop to c5. Play d4 anyway.
Again two captures, and again one of them is a mistake.
Pawn takes is the mistake.
Bishop takes f7, check. The same sacrifice.
The king takes, and queen to h5 checks and hits the bishop on c5 at the same time.
Black blocks. You take the bishop back. Material's level, and Black's king is out in the open. The engine says about plus one.
Black guards d4. Knight to f3 hits it again.
Black hits your queen with d6. Go forward, with check.
If the king steps to g7, take on d4.
With the knight, not the queen. The knight on c6 guards d4, so queen takes would lose her. You're a pawn up and Black's king is airy.

beats.reset: e4 e5 Bc4 Bc5 d4 exd4 Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qh5+ g6 Qxc5 Nc6 Nf3 d6 Qd5+
beats.say: But many players block with bishop to e6, hitting your queen. It's the losing move.
Knight to g5, check, and e6 is hit twice.
After king to e7, take the bishop. You're a piece up with the attack still going. If the king had gone to f6 instead, queen takes e6 mates soon.
Bishop takes is the right capture. This is the Lewis Gambit, and it's level. You just get an easy game.
Knight to f3 hits the bishop twice. Black guards it with the knight, and you trade.
Bishop to e3 sends the knight back. Then queen to g4 hits g7.
Black guards g7 with the queen. Knight to c3, eyeing d5.
Now d5 looks clever: it hits your bishop and opens the c8 bishop onto your queen. It's actually a mistake.
Queen to g3, still looking at g7. Not e2, where none of what follows works.
Black takes the bishop. Knight to d5 hits the queen, and threatens knight takes c7, forking king and rook.
If the queen covers c7 from d6, she stops guarding g7. Queen takes g7, and the rook on h8 is next.

beats.card: So how do you win with this?
beats.say: The whole opening in three lines.
One. Bishop to c4, aimed at f7. In nearly every trap today, that bishop pinned or covered f7.
Two. Keep the g1 knight home until the queen or the f-pawn has used the road. Castled king: bishop to g5. King in the middle: f4.
Three. Against knight f6 or bishop c5, d4 is the sharp choice. Know the wrong capture: knight takes e4, or pawn takes d4 against bishop c5.
These traps win quick games. They aren't the whole opening. A careful opponent reaches a level game, and then you have to think.
So play it against Stockfish next, and see which plan each game asks for.
